decisions.reason: The question asks whether highlighting helps programmers spot code that needs review. It leaves out how users edit suggestions and whether highlighting likely edits works better than highlighting low-probability tokens.
The method says the edit model highlights tokens likely to be edited. It omits the preliminary data from nine coders who corrected Codex outputs until the tasks were completed properly.
The poster gives the sample size and three easy LeetCode tasks. It omits the participants’ employer context and Python experience, along with randomization of task order and tool-to-task assignments.
The poster names the shared Davinci-002 Codex model, all three conditions, and both thresholds. It omits that the thresholds were chosen to match total highlight counts across the three tasks.

All three mean times and both p-values are correct, and the caption gives the 10-minute cap. The result leaves readers to infer that the comparison with generation probability was significant and that the comparison with prediction only was a trend.

Panel (b) shows the expected survival pattern. The poster gives no exact survival rates, does not define survival as a token remaining untouched, and does not explain how the pattern indicates more localized editing.
Panel (c) shows higher preference for Edit model highlights on an axis ending at 7. The poster omits the exact means, p-value, the three rating topics, and the reverse coding of distraction.
The poster omits that the edit model was trained on the same completions evaluated in the study and that comparable effects on unseen tasks remain unverified.
The poster does not state that effects on oversight accuracy and automation bias remain untested.
